texts: Many pieces and pawns attack each other. One capture, pin or fork can change everything.
The centre pawns are locked, so the game is decided on the wings by manoeuvres and pawn breaks.
An enemy knight or bishop sits on a square that none of your pawns can ever attack.
A piece has no defender or can be won by a smaller piece.
There is no pawn cover in front of a king while heavy pieces are still on the board.
A pawn with no opposing pawn in front or beside it is close to promotion.
The kings sit on opposite wings: both sides attack, and every tempo counts.
Before every capture, count the attackers and defenders of that square, then choose the capture or the pawn break on purpose.
Name one pawn break for each side, then play for yours before you shuffle pieces.
Within three moves, plan a trade or a pawn move that removes the support of their outpost.
Before you move, list your undefended pieces and theirs, then protect one of yours or attack one of theirs.
Before you open any line, count the attackers near your king. Add pawn cover or castle first.
Put a piece in front of their passed pawn right away, or start a counter-attack that is faster.
Count the tempi: your pawn storm against theirs. Then choose attack or defence for the next three moves.
What did their last move change? What does it threaten?
Which structure or feature matters here (tension, a closed centre, an outpost, king safety, a loose piece)?
Which checks, captures and attacks does each side have?
Which line did you calculate to the end, and what is their best reply?
Say out loud what their last move changed before you touch a piece.
Name the pawn structure and the biggest weakness before you pick a plan.
Write down your checks, captures and attacks first, then choose.
Calculate their best reply to your move before you play it.

That’s a classic delusional “don’t memorize your opening” trap. You actually need proper theory.
Theory is not memorising for its own sake: it is knowing what the position wants. Run M first: what did their move change?
You’re one step closer to full clarity.
Under 2000, every game feels like chaos. Above it, it is calm: you know what the position asks. Every clean line moves you there.
Classic Blitz-junkie move: hoping for tricks instead of calculating.
Blitz trains your hands, not your head. Under 2000 Rapid, play Rapid and run MSPC on every move.
Slow down. The routine is four questions, not one guess.
That miss is information. Name the step you skipped, then try again.
Review one of your own games in Trim so the app can find your first Working Point.
Play ONE sparring game with “Be My Sparring Partner”: I will wait for the alarm signal on the board and test whether you punish it.
Trim that game and write down, in one sentence, what should have warned you. That sentence is your next Working Point.
